AI discoveries in biology

376 discoveries from 2020 to 2026

About AI discoveries in biology

This selection contains 376 catalog entries dated 22 Jan 2020 to 13 Nov 2026. 376 include structured evidence annotations describing reported tests, the AI contribution and remaining limits. Missing annotations mean those details have not been structured here, not that a study lacks evidence.

Dates follow the catalog publication policy. Coverage is selected and incomplete; entries can overlap or describe several results. Counts do not measure independent discoveries, clinical benefit or worldwide research output. Read the selection and evidence policy or compare catalog coverage by year and field.

13 Nov 2026Stanford University

Antibody design across observed and forecasted antigenic evolution

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: The Germinal Multi preprint abstract reports antibodies designed against several antigen variants at once. Experimental screens of tens of designs per campaign found binders to resistance-associated EGFR variants and neutralizers of historical SARS-CoV-2 variants, including variants withheld from design. Redesign of BD55-1205 restored neutralization of a forecast-guided engineered escape variant while retaining parental-variant activity. The escape result concerns an engineered variant, not a demonstrated future circulating strain. Review is limited to the abstract and original-server metadata.

Technology: Germinal Multi (computational antibody design framework); evolutionary forecasting model

Editorial relevance 67 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Preprint · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Germinal Multi computationally optimized one antibody paratope against multiple antigen variants, and an evolutionary forecasting model guided construction of an escape variant and antibody redesign.
Test and result
Tens of designs per campaign were screened experimentally; designs bound EGFR variants and neutralized SARS-CoV-2 variants, including variants withheld from the design process.
Limitation / still unknown
Review limited to the indexed abstract and publication metadata; full-paper methods and additional limitations were not assessed.

10 Nov 2026Amsterdam UMC

Machine learning reveals incomplete concordance between DNASE1L3 genotype and cfDNA phenotype

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Classifiers and UMAP analyzed 129,676 prenatal-test cfDNA samples, with genotype checks in 169 selected samples. The authors report fragmentomic profiles resembling DNASE1L3 R206C homozygotes in some non-homozygotes, while some confirmed homozygotes initially lacked the profile and acquired it in later pregnancies. This extends an already-known genotype association with phenotype discordance and within-person variation; it does not establish the mechanism or clinical utility.

Technology: Supervised classifiers; UMAP

Editorial relevance 53 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Classifiers and low-dimensional embeddings identified fragmentomic subgroups and discordant cases.
Test and result
Existing-cohort analysis with selected ddPCR genotype validation and a small longitudinal subset.
Limitation / still unknown
The validation cohort was enriched for discordance; general-population accuracy and causal interpretation remain unresolved.

10 Nov 2026Shanghai Jiao Tong University

Cross-state representation learning enables prospective discovery of dynamic protein allosteric sites

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: The preprint abstract reports that AllositeUltra recovered allosteric sites among its top three predictions in 65.2% of apo structures and 70.6% of substrate-bound structures. More importantly, application to MAGI2 identified a previously unrecognized interdomain pocket, tested by small-molecule screening and X-ray crystallography. This within-study experimental finding qualifies separately from the benchmark. Review is limited to the abstract and original-server metadata.

Technology: AllositeUltra (structure-aware protein language model combined with physical dynamics; residue-guided candidate supplementation)

AI contribution
A deep-learning model predicted allosteric sites on apo and substrate-bound structures and was applied prospectively to MAGI2 and proteome-wide.
Test and result
The predicted MAGI2 interdomain pocket was validated experimentally through small-molecule screening and X-ray crystallography; benchmark recovery was measured on apo and substrate-bound structures.

9 Nov 2026Harvard Medical School; Harvard College; New York Genome Center; Rush Alzheimer’s Disease Center, Rush University

TriSCOPE links cell-type-specific Alzheimer’s expression programs to inherited risk loci

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: TriSCOPE combined cell-level predictive modeling, donor-aware differential expression and pseudotime analysis across six single-nucleus RNA-sequencing datasets (about 4.2 million nuclei from 627 donors). It identified cell-type-specific predictively expressed genes that were often missed by univariate differential-expression analysis; conditional GWAS–eQTL colocalization supported 27 gene–cell-type pairs at Alzheimer’s risk loci, including pairs without significant differential expression. Selected gene signals and analytical branches were compared across independent cohorts.

Technology: TriSCOPE, using LightGBM-based multivariate predictive modeling integrated with differential expression and pseudotime analysis

Editorial relevance 53 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The supervised machine-learning branch prioritized gene-expression features that predicted clinical Alzheimer’s diagnosis within cell types, conditional on demographics and APOE genotype. The study integrated those model-ranked features with donor-aware differential expression, pseudotime and GWAS–eQTL colocalization to nominate genetically supported cell-type programs.
Test and result
Selected gene signals and analytical branches were compared across independent cohorts.
Limitation / still unknown
This is a computational reanalysis of previously published, post-mortem cross-sectional datasets; it did not collect new tissue or perform perturbation experiments. The authors state the framework is for feature discovery rather than clinical prognosis, cannot establish temporal ordering, and requires functional perturbation studies to distinguish pathogenic drivers from protective or reactive signals. The reported cell-level AUCs are modest and should not be presented as patient-level diagnostic performance.

9 Nov 2026University of Toronto

Generative design of de novo AAV vectors with unique serological profiles

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: The preprint abstract reports a variational autoencoder trained on natural AAV sequences to generate capsids. More than 255 designs were synthesized and tested in vitro. Seven transduced human cells at over 50% efficiency; four of those avoided neutralization by every AAV-reactive human serum sample tested, at the reported NT50 threshold below 1:50. This establishes in-vitro capsid properties, not in-vivo delivery or clinical efficacy. Review is limited to the abstract and original-server metadata.

Technology: Variational autoencoder (generative model of AAV capsid sequences)

Editorial relevance 67 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Preprint · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
A variational autoencoder learned AAV sequence constraints from natural sequences and generated functional capsid proteins de novo, with a second design campaign exploring uncertain regions.
Test and result
More than 255 AI-generated capsid designs were synthesized and tested in vitro; seven transduced human cells above 50% efficiency and four avoided neutralizing antibodies in all reactive human sera.
Limitation / still unknown
Review limited to the indexed abstract and publication metadata; full-paper methods and additional limitations were not assessed.

6 Nov 2026University of Miami; University of Toronto; University of Waikato; North Carolina State University

Random forests nominate fungal taxa associated with leaf-warming samples

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: An exploratory random forest identified three fungal sequence variants associated with warmed versus control leaf samples across six Florida plant species. Kondoa and Zasmidium candidates had lower mean counts in warmed samples, while a Cystobasidiomycetes variant had higher counts. Overall community richness and composition tests were null. These descriptive candidate associations do not establish differential abundance, causal taxon-specific warming effects or host-independent generalization.

Technology: Random forest; Boruta feature selection; naive Bayes taxonomy classifier

Editorial relevance 40 biology Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
A naive-Bayes classifier assigns sequence taxonomy; random forests and Boruta select three taxa informative for warming-treatment classification.
Test and result
Exploratory RF/Boruta feature selection and OOB classification on measured leaf-community counts, alongside paired conventional community tests.
Limitation / still unknown
Taxon-specific differential abundance, blocked host/plant robustness, causal effects and functional host/ecosystem consequences remain unestablished.

5 Nov 2026Texas A&M AgriLife Research; and Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis

AlphaFold-Multimer predicts 2,895 interactions among human mitochondrial proteins

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Texas A&M AgriLife Research screened 630,003 protein pairs from about 1,100 human mitochondrial proteins with AlphaFold-Multimer and identified 2,895 likely interactions, more than half not previously reported, giving 85 uncharacterized proteins their first probable partners. The paper appeared in Nature Communications on 25 August 2026 and the institutional release on 5 November. Lab experiments in yeast and human cells confirmed several of the partnerships; most predictions remain untested, and the disease links are potential targets, not established ones. Predictions are shared through the MitoMatch web tool.

Technology: AlphaFold-Multimer

Family AlphaFold: profile · models page

Editorial relevance 60 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
AlphaFold-Multimer predicted pairwise interactions among mitochondrial proteins; the predictions were released as the MitoMatch web resource.
Test and result
AlphaFold-Multimer screened about 630,000 protein pairs; lab experiments in yeast and human cells confirmed several of the predicted partnerships, while the release does not say how many of the 2,895 were tested.
Limitation / still unknown
Only several predictions were confirmed, most remain unverified, the interactions are described as likely rather than established, and disease links are potential targets.

4 Nov 2026Anthropic

First 3D structure of a prokaryotic vault particle, with Claude

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Claude searched protein databases, designed DNA constructs, reduced purification from about three days to about 90 minutes, and processed cryo-EM data into an initial model in 34 hours. The result is a particle made of 96 copies of a bacteriophage protein, with about 25% more internal volume than the mammalian version. Its biological function is unknown; this is a preprint, and Claude made errors that humans corrected.

Technology: Claude

Family Claude: profile · models page

Editorial relevance 67 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Preprint · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Claude searched protein databases, designed DNA constructs, optimized purification, and ran RELION cryo-EM processing to an initial model in 34 hours; it also made errors that humans corrected.
Test and result
The 3D structure was determined by cryo-EM; cryo-EM confirmed the vault shape for four of seven particle-forming proteins, and fifteen altered protein versions were tested, with a reviewer checking the structure.
Limitation / still unknown

2 Nov 2026University of California, Berkeley

Machine learning guided design of strong transcriptional activation domains

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: The preprint abstract reports computational generation of 500,000 candidate transcriptional activation domains and selection of 18,750 high-scoring sequences for yeast experiments using sequence-to-function models including three neural networks. More than 90% of 16,770 well-measured sequences functioned as activation domains. Some designed sequences retained activity in fungi, plants and human cells. Model agreement motivated the MADRIGAL consensus predictor. Review is limited to the abstract and original-server metadata.

18,750 selected sequences were tested experimentally in yeast; over 90% of 16,770 well-measured sequences functioned as activation domains, and some retained function in fungi, plants and human cells.

1 Nov 2026RIKEN Center for Sustainable Resource Science; Graduate School of Science, Technology, and Innovation, Kobe University

Machine learning guides yeast alcohol dehydrogenase specificity for trans-2-nonenal

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Researchers measured a training library of yeast alcohol dehydrogenase I variants, used support-vector activity regression/classification and a thermostability model to rank combinations, then tested 22 prioritized variants. Four showed higher specific activity toward trans-2-nonenal than wild type; LWFMY also showed improved thermostability under the study’s tests. The result is laboratory enzyme engineering, not an industrial process or validated product. The primary journal version was published 2026-11-01; a search result for an earlier-hosted copy had ambiguous date/provenance, so this entry does not claim it was the first public version.

Technology: Support-vector regression/classification models and docking-informed mutation selection

Editorial relevance 53 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Models trained on measured variant data ranked combinations in unexplored sequence space for experimental testing.
Test and result
The top 22 ranked variants were experimentally evaluated; four outperformed wild type on trans-2-nonenal, with one also improved in thermal stability.
Limitation / still unknown
Small selected validation set; specific activity differs from catalytic efficiency across substrate concentrations; ambiguous earlier-hosted copy means first-public date is not asserted.

29 Oct 2026Arc Institute; Stanford University

Evo 2 uses in-context learning to design de novo regulatory sequences with only tens of examples

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Arc Institute reports that Evo 2 designs functional regulatory sequences from 4 to 64 in-context examples without extra training, with 30-50% yield. Of nine AI-designed enhancers delivered by AAV to mice, seven drove detectable expression and two labeled layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons with 73% and 95% specificity. Results are bioRxiv preprints; in vivo work covers only layer 5 enhancers, and other designs (proteins, CRISPR loci, antibodies, phage genomes) are computational only.

Technology: Evo 2 (genomic language model); in-context learning; reinforcement learning post-training

29 Oct 2026Dartmouth College

A low-rank subspace of LLM representations carries most of their brain alignment

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: A Dartmouth preprint studied which language-model features predict human neural responses during naturalistic listening. Across three intracranial/fMRI datasets and six model conditions, reduced-rank regression recovered full linear encoding performance with about 1–3% of embedding dimensions. These directions differed from the embeddings’ principal variance axes and transferred across held-out participants, less strongly across datasets. This summary is limited to the abstract and affiliation/date metadata of the October 29, 2026 preprint. It concerns measured brain–model alignment, not proof that brains use the same representations.

29 Oct 2026Kimia Therapeutics

D2ML guided prospective ROS1 potency and selectivity optimization

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Assay-aware models were used to select 84 new compounds for synthesis and prospective testing in a ROS1 kinase program, with TRKB as an anti-target. The most selective prospective compound had a measured ROS1 IC50 of 14.7 nM and 233-fold selectivity over TRKB, compared with 20.3 nM and 79-fold for the most selective training-set compound. The evidence is biochemical and does not establish therapeutic efficacy or safety.

The authors prospectively synthesized and assayed 84 model-selected compounds. The most selective new compound had ROS1 IC50 14.7 nM and 233-fold selectivity over TRKB; the most selective training compound had 20.3 nM ROS1 IC50 and 79-fold selectivity.

AI contribution
After single substitutions were screened and activity-enhancing mutations experimentally validated, PIFS-PLM used 60–100 measured combinations to learn from selected ESM-2 features at active-site and conserved residues and predict beneficial combinations. Ten predicted LdTPS5 variants were tested; all were active, and the top variants substantially increased measured yeast product yield. The model also guided a selectivity optimization test. After experimentally screening activity-enhancing single mutants of LdTPS5, the researchers used PIFS-PLM, a few-shot model that selects features from protein-language-model embeddings using active-site and conserved-residue information, to propose mutation combinations.
Limitation / still unknown
The 73-fold result is product yield in the reported yeast system, reflecting effects of enzyme activity and expression; it is not a 73-fold increase in catalytic rate. The selectivity improvement was 15%. The model relies on a defined active site/conserved-site set and a small, enzyme-specific experimental dataset. Product profiles differed between cell-free extracts and yeast; these results do not establish universal performance across enzymes or production settings.

The classifier operated at a 33% false-discovery rate; the 135 ion traces were putatively annotated, and only four of 22 reconstructed reaction stoichiometries were experimentally validated. Therefore the full 11% result is a set of candidate activities, not 11% independently confirmed enzyme functions. The RihB activities were prompted by a low-confidence potassium-thymidine-adduct trace and then tested directly with purified enzyme; they should be distinguished from the classifier’s higher-confidence hit set.

The model integrated heterogeneous biomedical databases, encoded relational paths using a convolutional network and attention aggregation, and produced disease-target scores. 23 Dec 2025Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology

Machine-learning metabolomics prioritizes succinate in sepsis-associated encephalopathy

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: In plasma samples from 29 controls, 32 sepsis patients and 27 patients with sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE), LC–MS/MS plus machine-learning feature selection identified a 12-metabolite profile. Succinate rose stepwise from controls to sepsis to SAE, ranked among the five leading XGBoost features, and correlated with APACHE II, SOFA and lactate. In a cecal-ligation-and-puncture mouse model, dietary succinate supplementation before sepsis worsened cognitive-test performance, neuronal injury and microglial activation; succinate also increased inflammatory gene expression in cultured microglia.

Technology: Random forest and support-vector-machine feature ranking with XGBoost classification

Editorial relevance 60 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Machine-learning feature selection and classifier comparison were applied to the measured plasma metabolomics to identify discriminatory features; succinate ranked among the top five XGBoost features. Researchers then tested its functional relevance through supplementation in a mouse sepsis model and in cultured microglia. The animal/cell experiments were human-directed follow-up, not model-generated predictions.
Test and result
In a cecal-ligation-and-puncture mouse model, dietary succinate supplementation before sepsis worsened cognitive-test performance, neuronal injury and microglial activation; succinate also increased inflammatory gene expression in cultured microglia.
Limitation / still unknown
The human discovery cohort comprised 88 participants and the held-out model test set had 18 participants, so diagnostic performance and metabolite ranking need larger external cohorts. Succinate supplementation was given before CLP in mice, and cell experiments used a microglial cell line; these are preclinical perturbations and do not prove that succinate causes human SAE or that targeting it improves patient outcomes. Associations with severity scores are observational.

Limitation / still unknown
Use in practical applications is not reported in the abstract.

Editorial relevance 60 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
SONAR learned sequence-feature patterns associated with protein abundance in immune cells, including cell-type- and activation-dependent feature importance. Its outputs guided selection of 3′UTR motifs and synthetic sequence design; reporter assays and a CDK4-specific TCR construct then tested their effects on protein output and CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity. The model generated design hypotheses; the downstream experiments established the measured motif and T-cell results.
Test and result
Reporter assays found that CT-rich 3′UTR motifs increased protein output while AG-rich motifs were generally repressive.
Limitation / still unknown
The target-cell killing experiment used engineered CD8+ cells in vitro and three donors; no animal or patient treatment outcome was tested. Protein abundance prediction used limited cell and immune-subset datasets, and model feature importance is not itself causal evidence. The assay supports effects for the tested synthetic 3′UTRs and CDK4-specific TCR in the reported system, not all proteins or therapeutic settings.

CRG researchers measured more than 64,000 synthetic enhancers across seven stages of blood-cell development and found that enhancer combinations can activate genes in one cell type but repress them in another.
Limitation / still unknown
The enhancer designs are proof-of-concept reporter regulators, tested in mouse blood cells; this is not evidence of a safe or effective gene therapy. The paper's Cell page redirected to a cookie wall, so detailed findings rely on the CRG's linked official summary.

The GWAS, transcriptome-wide and colocalization results are statistical associations and candidate gene mappings, not proof of causal mechanisms. Ancestry subgroup sizes differ, and results do not establish clinical utility or disease prevention. A 2025 author correction fixed a misspelling of AKNA as ANKA; it did not alter the reported analysis or findings.

The study then tested MCL1 dependence in ASPS using three distinct sgRNAs and murizatoclax; those experiments, rather than the prediction alone, provide the reported validation.
Test and result
The authors tested the prediction with CRISPR knockout and the MCL1 inhibitor murizatoclax in two ASPS cell lines; the reported viability effects were greater in ASPS than comparator tRCC lines.
Limitation / still unknown
bioRxiv preprint, not peer reviewed as stated by PMC. Validation was in two ASPS cell lines with CRISPR and inhibitor assays; it does not establish patient benefit or clinical efficacy. The model nominates dependencies and is not a functional screen itself.

Finding: The CODA platform used the Malinois deep-learning model and sequence-search algorithms to design synthetic cis-regulatory elements (CREs). In massively parallel reporter assays, 94.1% of the synthetic sequences met the authors’ cell-type-specificity criterion, versus 73.6% of model-selected natural sequences and 40.6% of chromatin-mark-selected natural sequences; synthetic sequences also had higher measured target/off-target separation across K562, HepG2 and SK-N-SH cells. One neuron-directed sequence, synN1, retained cortical and neuronal expression in mice, including postnatal neocortical layer 6 and subplate neurons.

Technology: CODA (Computational Optimization of DNA Activity) with Malinois deep neural network and AdaLead, simulated annealing, and Fast SeqProp sequence search/design algorithms

Editorial relevance 60 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
Malinois predicted MPRA activity of candidate DNA sequences in K562, HepG2 and SK-N-SH cells; CODA iteratively optimized sequences for specified cell-type specificity. Researchers synthesized and experimentally measured the designs by MPRA, then tested selected CREs with reporter constructs in zebrafish and mice. The paper attributes the novel sequences and their measured expression specificity to this model-guided design loop.
Test and result
In massively parallel reporter assays, 94.1% of the synthetic sequences met the authors’ cell-type-specificity criterion, versus 73.6% of model-selected natural sequences and 40.6% of chromatin-mark-selected natural sequences; synthetic sequences also had higher measured target/off-target separation across K562, HepG2 and SK-N-SH cells.
Limitation / still unknown
The in-vitro work used three transformed human cell lines and reporter assays. In-vivo testing covered a small selected set: two of three liver-directed and two of three neuron-directed elements were active in zebrafish; mouse validation focused on neuronal synN1, with n=3 synN1 mice for postnatal cell-type analysis and n=6 for the 5-week cortical reporter assay. These are transgenic reporter results, not therapeutic delivery or evidence of clinical utility. Earlier synthetic enhancer studies existed; this paper’s counted result is its CODA/Malinois comparison against natural sequences plus selected vertebrate validation, not the general idea of AI-designed enhancers.

CRISPR perturbation and Bayesian network inference map immune-disease regulatory cascades in primary CD4+ T cells

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: The study used CRISPR knockouts of 84 genes in primary human CD4+ T cells and a new linear latent causal Bayes (LLCB) network-inference method to estimate 211 regulatory connections. Integrating the inferred network with immune GWAS analyses identified an interconnected module in which KMT2A was inferred upstream of JAK-STAT and IL-2 signaling regulators including IRF4, STAT5A/B and IL2RA, linking an epigenetic regulator to immune-disease-associated pathways.

Technology: Linear latent causal Bayes (LLCB), a Bayesian extension of linear latent causal network inference, applied to CRISPR knockout and RNA-sequencing data

Editorial relevance 60 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
LLCB inferred direct and indirect regulatory relationships from perturbation-associated expression effects across 84 targeted genes. The model-derived network and gene-program analysis, combined with immune GWAS statistics, supported the specific KMT2A-to-JAK-STAT/IL-2 regulatory finding. CRISPR perturbation supplied the experimental perturbation data; the network algorithm converted those measurements into the reported regulatory map.
Test and result
The study used CRISPR knockouts of 84 genes in primary human CD4+ T cells and a new linear latent causal Bayes (LLCB) network-inference method to estimate 211 regulatory connections.
Limitation / still unknown
The study perturbed 84 selected genes in primary CD4+ T cells from three donors, so this is not a complete T-cell regulatory map. LLCB “direct effects” are statistical effects adjusted for other perturbed genes and are not evidence of physical binding; effects from unperturbed genes can be attributed to modeled edges. The GWAS integration identifies pathway links, not proof that the inferred cascade causes clinical disease. A prior bioRxiv version (10.1101/2023.09.17.557749) is the same study and is not counted separately.

AI contribution
RoseTTAFold2-Lite used residue–residue coevolution and predicted complex structures to rank candidate protein pairs in a proteome-wide screen. About 470 calls from 101 callers to 117 receivers were analyzed, and playback experiments showed elephants respond more to calls addressed to them.
Limitation / still unknown
More data are needed to isolate the names, it is unknown whether elephants name other things, and naming was not universal.

Test and result
Expression analyses in separate public sepsis transcriptome cohorts supported several markers, and qRT-PCR in cecal-ligation/puncture and LPS mouse models found increased neutrophil expression of those five genes.
Limitation / still unknown
The single-cell discovery comparison was very small (four sepsis cases and two controls) and the two clusters are analysis-derived states in this dataset; the study does not establish that they are distinct universal neutrophil lineages. AI contribution
Personalized community metabolic models estimated strain-level contributions to secreted metabolites in human iHMP samples. In a DSS-induced mouse colitis experiment, oral administration of the bacterium or metabolite improved reported colitis measures.

Deep-learning knee imaging phenotypes reveal osteoarthritis genetic and fracture associations

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Using knee DXA scans from the UK Biobank, a ResNet-101 model identified 1,931 more probable knee-osteoarthritis cases than health-record coding and a U-Net segmentation model estimated minimum joint-space width (mJSW). In 29,257 participants, the quantitative mJSW phenotype had substantially higher SNP heritability than the binary phenotypes and yielded 18 genome-wide-significant loci, compared with one for the image-based binary classifier and six for ICD-10 coding; only one mJSW locus was already significant in a large prior knee-OA GWAS. Technology: ResNet-101 convolutional neural network for knee-OA classification and U-Net image segmentation for joint-space measurement

Editorial relevance 53 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The neural networks converted routine knee DXA scans into two disease phenotypes: a case–control OA classifier and a quantitative minimum joint-space-width measurement. The researchers used these AI-derived phenotypes in GWAS and downstream epidemiological association analyses, increasing statistical power and revealing genetic and fracture associations that were not significant with ICD-10 case coding or the binary classifier.
Test and result
Using knee DXA scans from the UK Biobank, a ResNet-101 model identified 1,931 more probable knee-osteoarthritis cases than health-record coding and a U-Net segmentation model estimated minimum joint-space width (mJSW).
Limitation / still unknown
The GWAS used 29,257 quality-controlled UK Biobank participants with knee DXA images, all from the analyzed white-British ancestry subset; ancestry transferability is unestablished. DXA images were non-weight-bearing. The 18 loci are genome-wide associations for a model-derived quantitative endophenotype, not 18 proven causal OA genes; the paper notes only one also reached significance in a previous large knee-OA GWAS and many loci overlap broad anthropometric associations. The fracture result is observational and does not show that OA or joint-space narrowing causes fractures. The medRxiv preprint DOI 10.1101/2023.03.07.23286909 is an earlier version of this same study and is not counted separately.

12 Jun 2023Gladstone Institutes; University of California, San Francisco; Chan Zuckerberg Biohub San Francisco

SIMMER-guided experiments identify gut bacterial strains that deplete methotrexate

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: SIMMER combines reaction-chemistry and protein-sequence similarity to predict gut microbial species and enzymes responsible for drug biotransformations. For methotrexate (MTX), the model predicted candidate strains and enzyme sequences; researchers tested 42 gut bacterial isolates by HPLC. SIMMER predicted 13 isolates as MTX-metabolizing, and 10 of those tested isolates showed MTX depletion; the association was significant in the study (Fisher exact p=0.046). Predicted MTX-hydrolysis enzyme signatures were also enriched in stool samples of MTX nonresponders in an analyzed rheumatoid-arthritis cohort.

Technology: SIMMER, a computational reaction-similarity and protein-homology pipeline using chemical fingerprints, MetaCyc reactions and gut metagenomic sequences

Editorial relevance 53 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
SIMMER proposed specific bacterial species and enzyme sequences for known drug transformations. The team tested its MTX predictions against an independent panel of 42 gut bacterial isolates and HPLC-measured drug depletion, and compared predicted enzyme presence with baseline stool metagenomes and later MTX response in an RA dataset.
Test and result
For methotrexate (MTX), the model predicted candidate strains and enzyme sequences; researchers tested 42 gut bacterial isolates by HPLC.
Limitation / still unknown
The study reports species-level evidence for bacterial MTX depletion, but the enzyme predictions themselves were not individually purified or functionally validated. Only 13 of 42 tested isolates were predicted positive and 10 depleted MTX; predictions may have false positives, as the authors note. The RA association is observational and does not establish that microbial metabolism caused treatment nonresponse. The underlying fact that gut bacteria can metabolize MTX was already known; this result concerns species-level prediction and validation, not discovery of MTX metabolism itself.

Editorial relevance 60 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The model built context-specific networks from single-cell data, simulated transcription-factor loss, and prioritized noto and lhx1a for experimental follow-up. Researchers used CRISPR/Cas9 crispants, single-cell RNA-seq and marker assays to test the predicted zebrafish cell-fate effects; the prechordal-plate increase after noto loss was reported as previously unrecognized.

A later unreviewed 2024 preprint raises implementation and benchmarking concerns, particularly about its use of ATAC-seq for distal regulatory interactions and comparisons with other GRN tools; this record relies only on the specific perturbation predictions tested experimentally and does not adopt the paper's broader benchmarking claims.

6 Mar 2022University of Valencia; Spanish National Research Council; University of Sussex

Generative models estimate higher-order plant co-occurrence patterns

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: A generative model fitted to 5153 observed plant patches in four Spanish dryland communities estimated that conditioning on additional species often weakens positive lower-order co-occurrence associations, with species-specific exceptions. The conditional frequencies were estimated from model-generated patches, not 300000 field observations. This is a descriptive relationship in a learned distribution; it does not establish causal ecological interactions or actual succession.

Technology: Generative adversarial networks fitted to species-presence distributions

Editorial relevance 40 biology Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
GANs learn the high-dimensional joint distribution of plant presence and supply conditional co-occurrence estimates that describe how associations change when additional species are present.
Test and result
GAN models learned joint species-presence distributions from 5153 recorded vegetation patches. Generated composition abundance and soil-affinity patterns were compared with the observed data; higher-order conditional association estimates were derived from generated configurations.
Limitation / still unknown
The specific third- and fourth-order conditional frequencies were not independently checked in held-out field data. Generated patches and repeated model initializations are not independent field replication. Co-occurrence does not prove competition, facilitation or other mechanisms. VAE-generated succession, pioneer rankings and restoration benefits are outside this record; reconstruction accuracy is not ecological forecast accuracy.

8 Jun 2021University of Oxford; University of Coimbra; University of North Carolina at Greensboro; University of Algarve; Gorongosa National Park

Satellite-image clustering guides discovery of four late Miocene fossil sites in Mozambique’s Urema Rift

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: Unsupervised k-means clustering of seven Landsat 8 spectral bands highlighted a small set of priority areas for paleontological field survey in Gorongosa National Park. The 2018 campaign documented four new late Miocene fossil localities; three lay within the model’s target cluster and the fourth was less than 90 m away in the same gully system. Together, the sites expose the first reported estuarine coastal-forest fossil setting in the East African Rift System, filling a regional paleoenvironmental gap.

Technology: Unsupervised k-means clustering of Landsat 8 imagery

Editorial relevance 60 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The authors clustered seven spectral bands without pre-labeled land-cover classes, compared clusters with known fossil localities, and selected the cluster containing most known sites as a predictive target for field prospecting. This decision-support workflow directed the 2018 field survey that documented the new localities; a random forest was separately used to estimate spectral-band importance.
Test and result
Unsupervised k-means clustering of seven Landsat 8 spectral bands highlighted a small set of priority areas for paleontological field survey in Gorongosa National Park.
Limitation / still unknown
This was a pilot study in a 36 km² area and the model had notable false positives: reported precision was 55.56%, despite 84.6% overall accuracy. Three of four new localities overlapped the selected cluster; the fourth was less than 90 m away and was found by surveying the same gully system, so model localization for that site is indirect. The findings are four new fossil localities, not four new hominin taxa; the reported estuarine coastal-forest interpretation is a paleoenvironmental inference.

Learned screening helps identify pralatrexate antiviral activity in cell assays

The study found antiviral activity for pralatrexate in cell assays. This is an in-vitro drug-repurposing result, with no established effectiveness or safety as a COVID-19 treatment; the computational target hypothesis does not by itself establish the cellular mechanism.

Four drugs selected after a hybrid learned-model and simulation screen underwent laboratory evaluation, including direct cell-assay evidence for pralatrexate activity. This is not clinical efficacy.

Patient efficacy, therapeutic window for this infection and definitive cellular target mechanism remain unestablished.

21 May 2020University of California, Berkeley; Monash University; University of Melbourne

AcRanker-guided discovery of AcrIIA20 and AcrIIA21 anti-CRISPR proteins

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: AcRanker, an XGBoost ranking model using amino-acid sequence features, ranked proteins from prophage regions in self-targeting Streptococcus genomes. Experimental testing identified two previously unknown type II-A anti-CRISPRs: AcrIIA20 (ML1), which strongly inhibited Streptococcus iniae Cas9 and weakly inhibited S. pyogenes Cas9, and AcrIIA21 (ML8), which inhibited S. pyogenes, S. aureus and S. iniae Cas9 with lower potency.

Technology: AcRanker, an XGBoost pairwise ranking model trained on amino-acid composition and grouped di- and tri-mer features

Editorial relevance 60 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The model ranked candidate proteins from predicted prophage regions for anti-CRISPR likelihood; the researchers selected candidates from those rankings and biochemically tested them. It directly prioritized the proteins later named AcrIIA20 and AcrIIA21, whose Cas9 inhibition was measured in vitro.
Test and result
Experimental testing identified two previously unknown type II-A anti-CRISPRs: AcrIIA20 (ML1), which strongly inhibited Streptococcus iniae Cas9 and weakly inhibited S. pyogenes Cas9, and AcrIIA21 (ML8), which inhibited S. pyogenes, S. aureus and S. iniae Cas9 with lower potency.
Limitation / still unknown
The authors selected 10 candidates for follow-up, successfully purified nine and reported three validated candidates across their experiments, including ML3/AcrIIA12, which had also been identified separately as an LmoCas9 inhibitor during the study. AcrIIA20 and AcrIIA21 were roughly tenfold less potent against SpyCas9 than the established AcrIIA4 control; tested potency and host range are assay-specific. The 2025 Evo paper reports distinct generated proteins EvoAcr1–5 and separate assays; shared anti-CRISPR function does not make these identical discoveries.

KCML links olfactory-receptor perturbations to multicellular organization and colorectal-cancer signaling

In colorectal-cancer cells, it associated depletion of olfactory receptors and TGFβ/WNT pathway genes with abnormal multicellular organization. Test and result
Knowledge- and Context-driven Machine Learning (KCML) analyzed perturbation phenotypes across molecular, cellular and population scales.

Patient data validate expression associations and outcome stratification, not a causal olfactory-receptor mechanism in tumors. The authors describe KCML as hypothesis-generating; predictions can be indirect through interacting genes. This is a distinct paper/result from later AI cancer models.

22 Jan 2020University of California San Diego; and collaborators

Interpretable multi-omics machine learning reveals unexpected drug mechanisms in Huntington disease models

Source check: Source checked. Not independent scientific confirmation.

Finding: An interpretable machine-learning model integrated transcriptomic, epigenomic, metabolomic and proteomic data from Huntington-disease cell models to identify previously unknown mechanisms for protective compounds. The analysis predicted autophagy activation for one compound group and mitochondrial-respiration inhibition for another; follow-up imaging, biochemical and energetics assays experimentally confirmed these effects in the cell model.

Technology: Interpretable network-optimization model integrating multi-omics over a molecular-interaction network

Editorial relevance 60 biology Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

AI contribution
The model integrated multiple omics and prioritized cellular pathways as candidate mechanisms of action; researchers tested those predictions with cellular imaging, biochemical assays and energetics measurements. It revealed unexpected mechanisms for compounds with unrelated known targets.
Test and result
The analysis predicted autophagy activation for one compound group and mitochondrial-respiration inhibition for another; follow-up imaging, biochemical and energetics assays experimentally confirmed these effects in the cell model.
Limitation / still unknown
Findings were experimentally established in STHdhQ111 murine striatal cells, with autophagy effects also checked in human SH-SY5Y and HEK293 cell lines. The paper notes that the model prioritizes pathways but does not resolve every causal step or demonstrate therapeutic efficacy in patients.
